text: ARC gives me some hope for 3rd player on the GPU market. Though even with driver improvements, I would like to pour a bit of a cold water on people in comments - yes, their GPU's are cheap. But when they have competitive GPU's (especially from the beginning of a generation) - it's not like Intel will keep low prices. Once they have good GPU's, with good drivers and they will get some market share, those prices will become much, much more..... profit driven. Neither of 3 companies is a charity after all. The good thing is that competition between 3 companies (serious competition at least), has a chance of driving prices significantly lower than competition between 2 companies. And this is what I count on. If NVIDIA will feel that it is a default choice for most people - it won't feel the pressure. If AMD will feel that it is a prime choice for some and a good value option for most - it won't feel the pressure. That is why, once Intel has GPU's that are really competitive with drivers that are not worse to those of AMD or NVIDIA, we must be prepared to alter our purchasing choices. Imagine NVIDIA being default choice for only 30-40% of people. They would start panic. Ideally of course, no company should feel like it is default choice for anyone, but world is far from ideal.

text:
Intel is coming from way, way behind in the GPU race.  Those specs make for a GPU with 170% the compute power of the RX 6600.  RDNA, of course, made a pretty big leap forward in performance scaling over GCN, but Intel is actually still way behind that.  Vega scales about 40% better than the A580 does, when comparing shader count and clock speed.  RDNA 2 is shown here scaling >70% better.

So in those rare games where the Intel card is faster, that's just a dim glimpse of what it should be.

I don't think they'll be able to make up enough room with driver improvements.  Most of these scaling inefficiencies are baked into the architecture.  But they should be able to claw some more performance out of the Arc cards in the future - just not nearly enough to make them catch up in a big way to AMD or nVidia.

Conclusion A: The 3050 was horrible to begin with, is still a waste of silicon and the fact that people still buy that thing is laughable. Only that it's Nvidia's bean-counters doing the laughing part.

Conclusion B: AMD and Nvidia seriously need to stop cheaping out on PCIe and memory bandwidth. The fact that a x16 interface and 256bit memory controller become the A580's saving grace speaks for itself.

Conclusion C: If Intel doesn't get the driver stack working way better (and most importantly consistently) by the time Battlemage launches, and better launches soon, it'll probably be game over for Arc. They simply won't be able to sell another generation of GPUs below cost. The A580 has the same ACM-G10 die as an A770. That's 406 mm² of TSMC N6 worth of silicon. The 7600 uses half of that and pretty much roflstomps the A580 as it sees fit. And TSMC's N6 yields are excellent, these dies can't all be salvage.
They have to get their sh*t together or Pat Gelsinger will have no choice left but to ax the project.

If I were on windows (I am not) I would make the following performance calculus at equivalent pricing.
AMD (100%)
Nvidia (95%)
Intel (80% at the realistic worst case)

The reason the difference for AMD vs Nvidia is little because of my personal distaste for the way they are pushing for a closed vendor-locked ecosystem and them being by far the biggest vendor (Those are very much personal considerations). But I will still consider the obvious benefits where DLSS can be acceptable FSR2 is not, I may even prefer FSR1 for it's problems are less distracting. Better RT performance so far has been a minor thing as I put more emphasis on Looking decent at a good framerate than Looking good at a decent framerate.

As for Intel, because of its hit-and-miss nature I would require all games I want to play to at least run decently, so the averages are not as important, as long as the lower bound is decent. If I wanted to play starfield and find out it is broken on ARC or even some older game, that is just not acceptable as long as there are other options. One or two is acceptable but the problems are in more than that. 

Of course I am not running on Windows, as it stands Nvidia's linux drivers are just a pain to deal with, and the bare standard of having a mixed refresh rate with multi monitor variable refresh rate work is just not met on linux with Nvidia. And because of that it's really a non-starter.

Intel, AMD and Nvidia have all done it before, and they'll do it again.

@w04h  Look at Vega 56 and Vega 64.  Both had amazing compute performance and rubbish gaming performance.

Because they were optimised for Datacentre/workstation, not gaming.  No amount of driver optimisation could overcome the fact that they were primarily designed to compute, not to game.

Alchemist is a Datacentre part that was never properly "retrofitted" for gaming.  No amount of driver optimisation will make it perform as well in games as it does in compute.

Nvidia makes twice as much money from Datacentre as it does gaming. Low volume , high margins - it's much easier and much lower risk.

It's gaming GPU's are not a high priority.  None of the three figures gaming as a high priority, in fact - AMD and Intel are both trying to get the Datacentre market.  None of those companies see gaming as anything other than a side hussle.  Which is why we're seeing such dismal generational improvements - the gaming market is not their focus.

Battlemage will probably be far better optimised for gaming, but it's still a Datacentre architecture first, a gaming architecture second.
